name: bull

attributes.attribute: symbol of ferocity and of agricultural abundance
Continental god connected to the bull
a transformed swineherd whose bull is central to the Táin
the white-horned bull of Ailill mac Máta

text: The bull is a symbolic animal in Celtic tradition. Its image appears across Europe before the rise of the Celts. The figure may come from the pre-Celtic past. The Celts took up the bull in image and in story. They joined it to ferocity on one side and to agricultural plenty on the other. Some Continental sanctuaries show traces of bull sacrifice. Bull skulls sometimes guarded the entrances of shrines. The god Esus was tied to the bull and could appear as a woodsman cutting trees among bulls. Some scholars read the tree and the bull as paired images of sacrifice. The bull stands for strength and ferocity in Irish texts. The great cattle raid of the Táin Bó Cúailnge on Ulster begins because of a bull. That bull, Donn Cúailnge, was a transformed swineherd. Its only equal was the white-horned bull Finnbennach of Ailill mac Máta, also a transformed swineherd. The bull as a sign of plenty joins the wider weight of cattle among the herding Celts.

okr.objective: Describe the bull as a Celtic symbolic animal tied to ferocity, abundance and cattle culture.
key_results: The bull image appears across Europe before the Celts and may be pre-Celtic.
Some Continental sanctuaries show traces of bull sacrifice and bull-skull shrine guards.
The god Esus was connected to the bull and could appear as a woodsman.
In the Táin Bó Cúailnge the cows of Ulster are raided because of the bull Donn Cúailnge.
